title: Human-in-the-Loop & Agent Guardrails
subtitle: The badge worked, and now your manager is drowning. A second reader, a confidence dial, and how to ask a person well.

objectives.title: Add a Second Reader
objectives.description: Use a second AI call that never writes: it reads each answer and says, 0 to 100, how sure it is that the answer can go out with nobody looking.

objectives.title: Set a Confidence Threshold

activities.title: The Dial
activities.description: About 20 minutes in the notebook, Parts 1 to 4:

steps.title: The tray is full (5 min)
steps.description: Your AI employee answers 8 messages. With last week's badge, every answer to an outside person waits for the manager. Bet: how many of the 8 really need a person?

steps.title: Hire a second reader (5 min)
steps.description: A second AI call that never writes. It reads each answer and scores it 0 to 100: how sure is it that this can go out with nobody looking?

steps.title: Set your dial (9 min)
steps.description: Pick the bar. Add always_ask("word") rules. The answer key shows ✅ handled alone, 🟡 right call, 🥱 wasted and 😬 slipped. Aim for zero slipped and as few wasted as you can, then write why.

activities.title: Break a Dial, Build Your Own

steps.title: Trap your neighbor's dial (7 min)
steps.description: One calm, friendly message aimed at their company and their bar. If the answer goes out alone, your neighbor decides: would their manager be fine with it?

steps.title: Your final project's dial (6 min)
steps.description: What your agent does alone, when it stops and asks, who it asks, how many times a day, and what it always asks about. An AI plays that person. The blue box goes into HW #9.

takeaways.text: A human in the loop is not a guardrail. A human who is paying attention is. Send a person 150 approvals a day and you get a rubber stamp. Send fewer, better questions.
The dial is a business decision. Set the bar too low and something slips out that needed a person. Too high and your manager reads everything again. The AI doesn't pick the bar. You do.
Tone is not risk, and friendly is not safe. A word list reads words. A second reader reads meaning. It can still be confidently wrong, which is what always-ask rules are for.
Rules for what you already know. A second reader for what you don't. A person for what matters. And when you ask a person, show them who is asking, what will happen, and whether it can be undone.
